name: Humoral theory
summary: Health as a balance of four bodily fluids: a Greek idea that ruled learned medicine for some two thousand years and still underpins Unani practice today.
body: The theory held that the body contained four humours, blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile, and that health was their proper balance. Each humour was paired with two of the qualities hot, cold, moist and dry, with an element, a season and a stage of life, so that one scheme could explain a fever, a gloomy temperament and why the old were thought cold and dry. Illness meant that a humour was in excess or deficit; treatment meant restoring balance through diet, purging, vomiting or letting blood.

The idea took shape in the Hippocratic writings of classical Greece and was systematized by Galen in the second century CE, who built a theory of temperaments on the four qualities. Its strength was coherence: it tied the body to the seasons and the cosmos and gave every symptom a reason. Scholars of the Islamic world, for whom Galen and Hippocrates were the pre-eminent authorities, ordered the Greek material into encyclopedias. Ibn Sina's *Canon*, which counted the humours among the material causes of health and sickness, was printed more than thirty-five times in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries alone.

Humoral thinking underpinned European medicine, and everyday speech, Shakespeare's included, until at least the 1700s. It faded slowly rather than being refuted at a stroke; only in the late nineteenth century was its signature therapy, bloodletting, discredited for most ailments. It never vanished entirely. Unani medicine, brought to India by Arabic-speaking physicians and recognized today by the Indian government for clinical practice, still rests on the humoral theory.

confidence.note: That humoral theory dominated Greek, Islamic and European learned medicine is undisputed. Its end has no single date: it declined over the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, and in Unani medicine it is still taught.

name: Miasma
summary: Disease as a poison in the air, rising from marshes, filth and rot: wrong about the cause, yet a powerful argument for drains and clean cities.
body: Long before anyone could see a microbe, physicians noticed that sickness clustered in particular places: low marshy ground, stagnant water, crowded and stinking streets. The Hippocratic treatise *Airs, Waters, and Places* (c. 400 BCE) told a doctor arriving in a strange city to study its winds, its exposure to the sun and whether its waters were marshy. The Roman architect Vitruvius warned against building near marshes, whose morning fogs, charged with the breath of swamp creatures, spread an unwholesome effluvia over the inhabitants. Bad air, or miasma, was the natural explanation.

The idea travelled with Greek medicine. Ibn Sina listed airs among the causes that change and preserve the condition of the body, and the choice of air became part of every regimen of health. It was not a foolish theory. Foul smells often did mark real danger, and miasma explained why epidemics struck some districts and spared others, without needing any agent that no one had ever seen.

Miasma reached its height in the nineteenth century. When John Snow argued in 1849 that cholera entered the body through the mouth, the accepted view was that it was airborne, and in the mid-1800s many people still held that diseases were caused by bad air. Reformers who believed it pressed for drains, sewers and clean streets, measures that helped even where the reasoning behind them was mistaken. The microbes of Pasteur and Koch displaced the theory, though not overnight, and by the last decades of the century it had lost the argument.

confidence.note: The prevalence of bad-air explanations from the Hippocratics to the mid-nineteenth century is well documented in primary texts. Its decline was gradual: many sanitarians held on to it for years after Snow and Koch, so any end date is approximate.

name: Bloodletting
summary: Opening a vein to drain excess blood: one of the longest-lived treatments in medicine, abandoned as a cure-all only in the nineteenth century.
body: For more than two thousand years, removing blood was among the most common things a physician did. Its logic came from humoral theory: if illness meant an excess of a humour, the remedy was to take some away, and blood was the easiest humour to reach. Bloodletting was already a common treatment by the first century CE, and when Galen declared blood the dominant humour it gained still greater weight. Practitioners opened veins with lancets and fleams, or bled locally with cups and leeches.

Physicians of the Islamic world and medieval Europe inherited Galen's authority and the procedure with it, and bleeding reached its peak in Europe in the nineteenth century. In Paris, François Broussais traced fevers to inflamed organs and had leeches applied over them; France imported 42 million leeches for medical use in 1833 alone. In Philadelphia, Benjamin Rush bled patients heavily during the yellow fever epidemics of the 1790s, and George Washington was bled copiously in his last illness.

Doubt came from counting. In 1835 Pierre Louis compared pneumonia patients bled early in their illness with those bled later and found less benefit than expected. Contrary to legend, he did not condemn bleeding, only confined it to narrow limits, and Broussais's theories were already losing support. Pathology, the microscope and germ theory did the rest, and by the late nineteenth century bloodletting had been discredited for most ailments. It survives as phlebotomy for a few conditions, such as hemochromatosis and polycythemia vera.

confidence.note: The practice is abundantly documented from antiquity to the nineteenth century. What is debated is why it declined: Louis's figures mattered less than is often claimed, and changing theories of disease did much of the work.

name: Supernatural causes
summary: Illness as the work of gods, demons, sorcery or sin: probably the oldest explanation of disease, argued with by learned medicine but never wholly displaced.
body: In the earliest medical writing, disease often had an author. Babylonians and Assyrians attributed the deaths of mothers and infants to disease, demons or sorcery, and guarded against them with incantations, charms, amulets and prescriptions. Mesopotamian tablets from about 1800 BCE list omens that an incantation priest, the *āšipu*, consulted after examining a patient, and many Egyptian medical papyri include spells against diseases sent by angry gods. Such measures sat alongside herbs, potions, poultices and bandages, not in place of them.

Around 400 BCE the Hippocratic author of *On the Sacred Disease* attacked the idea head on. Epilepsy, he wrote, was no more divine than any other disease and had a natural cause; people called it divine out of ignorance and wonder, and those who cured it with purifications and incantations exploited that ignorance. Yet the same Greek world flocked to the temples of Asclepius, where the sick slept in hope of a healing dream.

Religious and natural explanations long coexisted. Early Muslim teaching held plague to be a mercy and martyrdom from God for the faithful and denied contagion, since disease came directly from God, though observation of contagion kept the question alive. In the eighteenth century Ottoman city-dwellers were still described as shunning smallpox inoculation as an interference with providence, and in 1680s England James II handed out gold touchpieces in a ceremony of healing by royal touch. Germ theory removed gods and demons from medical textbooks; it has not removed them from many people's understanding of why illness strikes.

confidence.note: Divine and demonic explanations are well attested in Mesopotamian, Egyptian, Greek and later texts. The current starts with writing only because earlier beliefs left no record; how far individual healers saw magic and medicine as separate is debated.

name: Spontaneous generation
summary: The belief that flies, worms and later microbes arise from mud, rot or broth. It took two centuries of experiments, ending with Pasteur's flasks, to kill it.
body: Maggots appear on rotting meat, worms in mud, mould on bread. For most of history the obvious conclusion was that such creatures arose from decaying matter itself. Aristotle, in fourth-century BCE Greece, gave the idea philosophical standing, ending his account of animal generation with creatures that arise 'spontaneously' rather than from parents. It mattered to medicine because it made rot creative: when Girolamo Fracastoro described seeds of contagion in 1546, he imagined them as spontaneously generated in certain kinds of putrefaction.

The challenge came by experiment. In 1668 Francesco Redi published evidence against spontaneous generation in insects, then a widely accepted Aristotelian idea, concluding that they were born from eggs laid by their mothers. But the microscope opened a new frontier. The animalcules teeming in infusions of plant and animal matter seemed to show that at least the smallest life still arose unbidden. Lazzaro Spallanzani repeated the infusion experiments of Needham and Buffon, showed their techniques were inadequate, and published his refutation in 1765. The argument was not settled.

It came to a head in France, where Félix Pouchet defended spontaneous generation in *Hétérogénie* (1859). Through the early 1860s Louis Pasteur answered with experiments, including swan-necked flasks that let in air but not dust or airborne microbes: sterilized broth stayed lifeless. The result reached far beyond biology. If microbes came only from other microbes, they could be traced, killed and kept out, the premise on which germ theory, antiseptic surgery and sterile technique were built.

confidence.note: The key experiments of Redi, Spallanzani and Pasteur are dated by their publications. Pasteur did not end all debate at once; some defenders held out into the 1870s, so the end date is approximate.

name: Qi and the channels
summary: Health as the smooth flow of qi through channels linking organs, body and cosmos: the framework of Chinese medicine for two thousand years, and still in daily use.
body: Chinese medicine built its picture of the body from ideas it shared with Chinese philosophy: *qi*, the stuff of which bodies and the world are made; yin and yang, paired and complementary forces; and the Five Agents, or *wuxing*. Warring States texts already tied qi, yin and yang to health and long life, and the *Zhuangzi* says that human birth is caused by the gathering together of qi.

Manuscripts from a tomb at Mawangdui, dated to 169 BCE, show a developed medical literature before the great synthesis. The *Huangdi neijing*, the Inner Classic of the Yellow Emperor, a complex and many-layered text probably compiled in the first century BCE, set out a systematic medical cosmology in which the body mirrored the state and the heavens. Health came from the balance of yin and yang, and qi flowed through channels, often called meridians in English, that linked the body's surface to its organs and their functions. This was not anatomy in the Western sense and did not try to be. It guided diagnosis by the pulse and treatment with needles, moxa and drugs.

The framework travelled. Buddhist priests carried Chinese medicine to Korea and Japan before the sixth century, and it spread more widely under the Tang. It survived the arrival of Western medicine, with early twentieth-century reformers such as Zhang Xichun insisting that philosophy was its very basis. Acupuncture has gained popularity worldwide since the 1970s, and research continues into what it can and cannot do.

confidence.note: Excavated manuscripts and the Inner Classic securely place the system's formation in the last centuries BCE, but the Inner Classic is a layered compilation and its exact date is debated. Claims of a much older origin rest on tradition.

name: The three doshas
summary: Ayurveda's theory that three doshas, vata, pitta and kapha, govern the body and that illness is their imbalance: ancient, hard to date, and very much alive.
body: Ayurveda describes the body through three *doshas*, vata, pitta and kapha, which are formed in varying combinations from five elements: air, water, space, earth and fire. Each governs a set of functions. In one modern summary, vata keeps things moving and eliminates waste, pitta regulates body heat, hunger and thirst, and kapha lubricates the joints, while catabolism, metabolism and anabolism are assigned to the three in turn. Health is a balance among them, and an imbalance between the three is a state of disease. Alongside the doshas sit seven bodily tissues and three waste products.

The classic statements are the great Sanskrit compendia. The *Charaka Samhita*, compiled by Agnivesha and edited by Charaka, covers the whole of Ayurvedic medicine, and the *Sushruta Samhita* covers surgery; both are still used by practitioners and have been carried into Tibetan, Arabic, Persian and other languages. Their dates are much debated, and so the birth of the idea can be placed only roughly. Writers often translate the doshas as 'humours', and the comparison with Greek humoral theory is tempting, though the two systems count and define their elements differently.

Unlike Europe's humours, the doshas never lost their institutional home. Ayurveda remains one of India's traditional health care systems, and about 240,000 American adults use it. In 2022 the government of India committed USD 250 million to a WHO Global Centre for Traditional Medicine. Rigorous evidence is thin, however, and some Ayurvedic preparations have been found to contain toxic amounts of lead, mercury or arsenic.

confidence.note: The three-dosha doctrine is central to the Charaka and Sushruta compendia, which practitioners still use. Those texts grew in layers and cannot be firmly dated; one review places Ayurveda's beginnings in the 2nd century BCE, others later, so the birth date is a broad estimate.

name: Human dissection
summary: Opening the dead to learn how bodies are built: tried at Alexandria, then abandoned for some fifteen centuries before returning in medieval Italy.
body: In early third-century BCE Alexandria, under the first Ptolemies, Herophilus and Erasistratus did something possibly unique in the Greek world: they systematically cut open human bodies. Alexandria offered an environment in which dissecting the dead did not meet with general disapproval, and Herophilus used it to distinguish the cerebrum from the cerebellum and trace nerves from the brain and spinal cord. The Roman writer Celsus later reported that the two men had also opened living criminals supplied by the kings, a charge that cannot now be checked.

Then the practice stopped. By Galen's time, in the second century CE, dissection even at Alexandria was restricted to animals, and Galen's animal-based anatomy became the authority for well over a millennium.

Human dissection returned in the universities of northern Italy. Bodies were opened to find the cause of death from the 1280s, and in Bologna in 1315 or 1316 Mondino de' Luzzi anatomized a woman's corpse; his *Anatomia*, completed in 1316 and apparently meant to be read aloud while others did the cutting, dominated teaching for two hundred years. In 1543 Vesalius's *Fabrica*, built on his own careful dissections, began to correct Galen.

A popular story holds that the medieval Church forbade dissection. It issued no general ban. Pope Boniface VIII's bull of 1299 forbade dismembering corpses and reducing them to bones, a funerary custom, was not aimed at anatomy and had no significant impact on it in Italy. The larger obstacles were the scarcity of bodies and public revulsion, which made the supply of corpses a recurring scandal into the nineteenth century.

confidence.note: The Alexandrian dissections are known only from later writers such as Celsus and Galen, and the vivisection charge cannot be verified. The medieval revival is well documented, though whether Mondino cut with his own hands is debated, and accounts differ between 1315 and January 1316 for his best-known dissection.

name: Germ theory
summary: The idea that specific living microbes cause specific diseases: guessed at in Rome, argued for in 1546, and proved in the laboratory between the 1860s and 1880s.
body: The notion of invisible living agents of disease is old. In the first century BCE the Roman scholar Varro, writing in his eightieth year, warned farmers that swamps bred minute creatures too small to be seen, which floated in the air and entered the body through the mouth and nose to cause serious diseases. In 1546 the physician Girolamo Fracastoro of Verona, in *De contagione*, described seeds of contagion (*seminaria*) that spread by direct contact, through objects such as clothing and sheets, or at a distance.

These were speculations, and historians resist making Fracastoro a prophet of microbiology. He could not clearly distinguish living from non-living particles and imagined his seeds arising spontaneously in putrefaction. For three centuries contagion competed with miasma, and in the mid-1800s many people still blamed bad air.

Proof came from the laboratory. Louis Pasteur showed that fermentation was the work of living organisms, attacked spontaneous generation through the early 1860s, and argued that microbes also caused infectious disease. He was not the first to say so, but his experiments gave the theory strong support. Robert Koch, a country doctor whose microscope was a gift from his wife, showed that the anthrax bacillus caused anthrax, published in 1876, laid down conditions for proving that a particular bacterium causes a particular disease, and in 1882 published his work on the tubercle bacillus. By the 1880s the theory was established, and it remade surgery, public health and the search for vaccines and drugs.

confidence.note: The laboratory proofs of the 1860s–1880s are thoroughly documented. How much Fracastoro or Varro anticipated modern microbes is a matter of interpretation; their particles were not microorganisms in the modern sense.

name: Fair tests of treatments
summary: Comparing like with like to see whether a treatment works: from Lind's scurvy sailors in 1747 to the randomised trial that became medicine's standard of proof.
body: For most of history a treatment's reputation rested on authority and on patients who seemed to get better. The fair test asks a harder question: better than what? Earlier precursors are often claimed, with varying justice. The Book of Daniel describes captive youths on a vegetable diet faring better than Babylonians on the king's food. Ibn Sina, around 1012, wrote that a drug's potency could be learned with certainty by experiment under stated conditions. In the seventeenth century Jan Baptist van Helmont dared the humoral physicians to take 200 or 500 fever patients, divide them by casting lots, and count the funerals. It was a challenge, not a trial.

In May 1747, aboard the *Salisbury*, the naval surgeon James Lind took twelve sailors with scurvy, as similar as he could find them, housed and fed them alike, and compared six remedies. Oranges and lemons worked fastest. Lind is rightly remembered, but he did not draw the clear lesson later credited to him, and his later writings still promoted other remedies. In 1835 Pierre Louis used numbers to question bloodletting in pneumonia, and others counted outcomes through the nineteenth century.

The decisive refinement was concealed random allocation. In the British Medical Research Council's 1948 trial of streptomycin for pulmonary tuberculosis, chance decided who received the drug, and those enrolling patients could not know the next assignment in advance. Its report became a methodological landmark, and the randomised controlled trial became the yardstick by which new treatments are judged.

confidence.note: Lind's trial and the 1948 MRC trial are documented in their published reports. Calling Lind's comparison the beginning is a convention: earlier proposals and comparisons existed, and Lind himself drew cautious conclusions.

name: Immunization
summary: Deliberately giving a mild infection to prevent a deadly one: a folk practice across Asia, Africa and Europe that became variolation, then vaccination.
body: Smallpox survivors did not catch it again, and people in many places learned to use the fact. The earliest written discussion of variolation in China appears in a book first published in 1549, and later Chinese manuals describe blowing smallpox material up a child's nose. In eighteenth-century Bengal, English residents watched itinerant Brahmins prick smallpox matter into the skin; claims that ancient Sanskrit texts describe the practice are not borne out by the texts. In Wales, where it was called buying the pocks, it was apparently in use by about 1600.

Learned Europe heard of it from the Ottoman world and from Africa. In 1714 a letter from Emanuel Timonius in Constantinople was read to the Royal Society, and in Boston Cotton Mather learned of inoculation from Onesimus, an enslaved African man in his household, who showed him the scar it had left. Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, wife of the British ambassador in Constantinople, described old women who opened a vein with a needle and inserted matter from a nutshell. She had her son inoculated there, and in April 1721, back in England, her daughter. The first inoculations in Britain and Massachusetts followed that year.

Variolation was far safer than natural smallpox but could still kill. Edward Jenner's use of cowpox, first tried on James Phipps in 1796 and published in 1798, removed that danger, and Pasteur later generalized the principle by weakening disease-causing microbes in the laboratory. The line from the old women of Constantinople runs to the eradication of smallpox.

confidence.note: Written evidence begins in China in 1549, but inoculation was a folk practice whose origins are unrecorded; claims of a much older Chinese or Indian invention rest on tradition. The eighteenth-century European adoption is well documented.

name: Eugenics
summary: The movement to 'improve' human heredity by controlling who had children: respectable science for half a century, it licensed forced sterilization and fed Nazi murder.
body: Francis Galton, a statistician and cousin of Charles Darwin, coined the word eugenics in 1883 and defined it as the study of agencies under social control that may improve or impair the racial qualities of future generations. He and his followers held that health and disease, intellect and character were largely inherited, and that a society could plan its breeding as farmers planned theirs. The idea borrowed the prestige of statistics and heredity, and drew strength from the racism, antisemitism, xenophobia and imperialism of its age.

In the early twentieth century eugenics was mainstream, backed by anthropologists, geneticists, social reformers and public health officials. In the United States, laws in 30 states led to the involuntary sterilization of at least 60,000 people judged unfit or feebleminded. In 1927, in *Buck v. Bell*, the Supreme Court ruled eight to one that Virginia could sterilize Carrie Buck. Nazi Germany took the logic furthest: a campaign of forced sterilization with at least 400,000 victims, and the killing of at least 70,000 disabled adults and 5,200 children, on the road to the Holocaust.

After 1945 the word became an embarrassment, but the practices lingered. North Carolina's Eugenics Board, created in 1933, approved the sterilization of an estimated 7,600 people before it was dissolved in the late 1970s, and some survivors were compensated by the state in the 2010s. Debates over prenatal screening and embryo selection keep the history in view.

confidence.note: The movement, its laws and court cases are thoroughly documented. Victim counts are minimums drawn from incomplete records, and eugenic practices did not end on a single date; some continued in other forms.

name: Informed consent
summary: The rule that patients and research subjects must freely agree, knowing the risks, to what is done to them: codified after medicine's worst abuses.
body: The principle that a person must agree, knowingly and freely, to what is done to their body was made a rule of medical research by catastrophe. From November 1946 to 20 August 1947 an American military tribunal at Nuremberg tried 23 defendants, all but three of them physicians, for crimes that consisted largely of medical experiments performed on concentration camp inmates against their will. The judges acquitted seven, convicted sixteen and sentenced seven to death.

Their judgment set out ten principles for permissible experiments, now called the Nuremberg Code. The first is that the voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential. The person must have legal capacity, be free of force, fraud, deceit or duress, and have sufficient knowledge and comprehension to make an understanding and enlightened decision. That last phrase is the seed of the word informed.

Writing a rule down did not make it practice. In the United States the Public Health Service's Tuskegee study, begun in 1932, followed 600 Black men without obtaining their informed consent and was shut down only in 1972, after information leaked to the public. The outcry produced the National Research Act of 1974, which required institutional review boards to approve human studies, and the Belmont Report, built on respect for persons, beneficence and justice. Today informed consent is standard practice for any medical procedure: a physician must explain what is proposed, its expected outcome and its risks.

confidence.note: The Nuremberg judgment and the US reforms of the 1970s are documented in official records. The current begins in 1947 because that is when consent was codified for research; earlier legal and administrative precedents existed but are not traced here.
